2. The predecessor of respondent Nos. 1 to 7 instituted O.C. Suit No. 61 of 1965 for declaration that the suit land appertained to his original C.S. khatian No. 27 and that the property recorded in the new Khatian No. 23 in the name of defendant No. 1 was wrongly prepared and that the same is liable to be recorded in his name in the rent roll Khatian No. 22. 

 3. The plaintiff's case is that the holding belonged to Agardi Sonaru who died leaving defendant No. 3 as heir. She made a gift of the holding to her only issue, the plaintiff in whose name it was recorded in the preliminary rent roll. On the basis of the gift the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land as his own for more than 40 years. Defendant No. 1 who has been living on the suit land as his licensee by erecting a hut filed an objection case in 1958 against the plaintiff. The notice of the objection case was never served upon the plaintiff. On the strength of the objection case defendant No. 1 succeeded in getting the suit land recorded in his name in a separate rent roll. He also filed a case under section 145 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the plaintiff. But in that case possession of the plaintiff was found. 

 4. The plaintiff paid rent of the holding to the Government from 1363 to 1369 B.S. In Chaitra, 1370 B.S. the tahsildar refused to accept rent from him on the ground that the suit land was recorded in the name of defendant No. 1. The plaintiff came to know of the fraudulent recording then and, therefore, filed the aforesaid suit. 

 5. The suit was contested.by defendant No. 1 His case was that the suit land was sold in auction and the landlord purchased it and also took delivery of possession. There after the landlord possessed the land in khas through the defendant as bargadar who subsequently took settlement of the said land from the landlord in 1355 B.S. Since then he has been in possession. The rent roll Khatian No. 23 has been correctly prepared. 

 11. None of these decisions, it seems, has considered the point involved, that is whether a gift of agricultural land is valid, from all the different aspect, The completion of an oral gift under Muslim Law takes place as soon as there, is a declaration of gift by the donee and delivery of possession of the property under the gift is made to the donee by the donor. Nothing remains to be done to make the sift a valid one enforceable under law. No reasonable answer coned be given as to why a gift of this nature should be further required to be effected by a registered instrument gad an oral gift, under Muslim Law remained imperfect unless something in writing was to make it a valid gift the question of registration might have arisen. This being not so in the case of such a gift, the requirement of a registered Instrument would seen to be redundant. On the other hand, if there is no oral gift but by an unregistered instrument a person seeks to make a gift of immovable property, it must be registered. When the performance of one kind of obligations imposed under a law makes certain act complete, a separate kind of obligation cannot be introduced to nullify the same unless expressly provided in another law. There are no degrees of completion. When an act is complete, nothing further is required to make it more complete. If, on the fulfillment or the three conditions mentioned above, an oral gift by a muslim of immovable property is complete, its completeness cannot be destroyed by the requirement of a register & instrument under section 260 as this has not been expressly applied to such gift. 

 13. Further, the learned Counsel for the appellant laid stress on the distinction between agricultural land and non-agricultural land and the different requirements of the two laws, regarding transfer of such land by gift. It may, however, be mentioned that there is no indication in section 129 restricting its application only to a particular class of lands, that is, non-agricultural land as section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1943 has provided. Section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act excludes from its operation only agricultural leases but not other dispositions. 

 14. So far as the wording of either section 26C of the Bengal Tenancy Act or section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is concerned, we do not find any reference to section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act which read with other sections of this Act contained contrary provisions relating to the requirement of registration of an instrument or gift by a Muslim. If the legislature intended to exclude the operation of section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act by the later enactment, it ought have expressly said so, or could have used some such expressions as notwithstanding anything contained in any ether law for the time being in force". Such phraseology or expressions are used by the legislature to give an enactment or some of its provisions an overriding quality and operation. One does not even have to look up other laws to find the use of such expressions. In section 90 as also in other sections of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act such expressions have been resorted to so as to impart superiority to its provisions over other laws. There is no such clause in section 89 of the Act or section 26C of B.T. Act which is under our consideration so as to exclude the operation of section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act in case of transfer of agricultural land. In addition, after the enactment of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act very little distinctions maintained between the incidents of agricultural land and non-agricultural land. For solid practical reasons also, no such distinction would seem to be attractive. If law as provided in section 129 has exempted the owner of urban property, which are generally more valuable than agricultural land, from transferring the same by a registered instrument, why should greater hardship be imposed on the holder of agricultural and by the requirement of a registered instrument for transferring his, interest therein by way of gift. Judged from different viewpoints, the effectiveness of an oral gift of immovable property when properly made has not been curtailed by the language of section 26C of the Bengal Tenancy Act or section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act insofar as it has been preserved by section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act. An oral gift of immovable property, whether it is agricultural land, or non-agricultural land, made according to the Muslim Law would, therefore be valid.
